profiles.meeting_scenario: At a large urban tertiary hospital, an acute care surgery attending and the director of perioperative operations are holding a brainstorming meeting after reviewing a recent multi-institutional study showing increased robotic use and lower conversion-to-open rates in emergent general surgery. The hospital already has an established elective robotic program, but emergency use is rare and informal. Their agenda is to generate candidate ideas for a 6-month internal pilot and associated quality-review proposal on whether robotic capability should be expanded for selected emergency general surgery cases, especially colectomies and hernia repairs. The expected outcome is not a final protocol, but a short list of promising pilot concepts, likely target cases, and a rough narrative they can bring to the surgery executive committee.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.role: Acute Care Surgery Attending and Robotic General Surgeon
members.expertise: Emergency general surgery, minimally invasive colectomy, robotic abdominal wall surgery
members.background: Trained in both acute care surgery and robotic general surgery at a high-volume academic center and joined the hospital two years ago to help modernize minimally invasive emergency care.
members.private_state: She wants to create a credible internal pilot that will let the acute care surgery service use robotics more often without triggering resistance from colleagues who think the robot is too slow or too resource-intensive for urgent cases.
hidden_assumptions: In emergency general surgery, a case still counts as an 'emergency' if the patient comes through the ED and needs surgery during the same admission, even when resuscitation allows the operation to happen the next morning.
The meaningful length-of-stay benefit from robotics is postoperative recovery time, because preoperative boarding and medical optimization are mostly unrelated to surgical approach.
A 'small pilot' naturally means restricting use to physiologically stable, imaging-defined cases that an experienced robotic acute care surgeon can selectively accept.
Unused or releasable elective robot block time can usually be redirected to urgent cases with informal service-line approval, so robot access is more a coordination issue than a policy barrier.

members.name: Michael Torres
members.role: Director of Perioperative Operations and Surgical Innovation
members.expertise: OR throughput, add-on scheduling, perioperative staffing, service-line implementation
members.background: A former perioperative RN with an MHA who now oversees OR utilization, robotic platform scheduling, and operational review for new surgical initiatives across the hospital.
members.private_state: He wants any pilot idea to look operationally defensible to hospital leadership, meaning it should improve throughput without depending on exceptions to current staffing or block-release rules.
hidden_assumptions: When surgeons say 'emergency cases,' they usually mean cases entering the true emergency add-on pathway and competing for same-day or overnight OR resources, not next-morning urgent inpatient cases.
A length-of-stay advantage only matters operationally if it shortens total hospitalization, because bed turnover and financial impact are driven by total LOS rather than postoperative LOS alone.
A 'pilot' should reflect the whole emergency service line, so all urgent colectomy and hernia cases should fall inside the tracking frame even if only some actually receive robotic surgery.

Robot use for unscheduled cases must fit existing staffing and room-allocation policies unless a formal exception is approved; elective robot blocks are not assumed to be available to emergency cases.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as an emergency case
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'emergency cases' or 'emergent general surgery cases' as the target population.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means index-admission acute care surgery patients who present urgently, including patients stabilized overnight and taken to the OR the next morning.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means cases routed through the emergency add-on workflow that require immediate or same-shift accommodation in OR capacity, especially nights and weekends.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'emergency case' is routine in both clinical and operational settings, and each interpretation sounds fully compatible with the study summary, so neither person feels a need to restate the boundary.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both cite the possibility of a 'shorter length of stay' as part of the value proposition.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of postoperative length of stay, since that is the portion most plausibly affected by surgical approach and mirrors the study's postoperative recovery signal.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of total hospital length of stay, because that is the number used in throughput dashboards and bed-management reviews.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both total LOS and postoperative LOS are standard hospital measures, and people often casually say 'length of stay' without specifying which one when discussing surgical quality papers.

misalignment_points.topic: Assumed robot availability for urgent add-ons
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss ideas that depend on 'using the robot when it's available' for urgent cases.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes that underused elective robotic time can be released or informally shared for selected acute care cases, especially next-morning add-ons.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes that no such block-sharing exists unless formally approved, so 'available' means fitting the case into current add-on staffing and room rules after the elective schedule is already set.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Neither person frames this as a disputed point; each treats their background operational context as already known, so 'if the robot's available' sounds like agreement while hiding different default scheduling worlds.

misalignment_points.topic: What is inside a small pilot
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree it would be safest to 'start with a small pilot' focused on colectomy and hernia cases.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a narrow clinical subset: stable patients with localized pathology, favorable imaging, and daytime staffing where robotic completion is realistically likely.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a service-line pilot frame that includes all urgent colectomy and hernia consults for monitoring purposes, even if many are later screened out from actually receiving robotics.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: People often use 'pilot' ambiguously to mean either a restricted treatment cohort or a broader implementation trial, and both versions sound prudent and incremental in a brainstorming meeting.

turns.inner_thought: That paper gives me enough cover to propose something modest and credible. I do not need a big emergency robotics program; I need a narrow internal pilot for acute care surgery patients who come in through the ED, get worked up and resuscitated, and then go to the OR during that same admission, often the next morning. If I frame it as a small pilot, people are less likely to react as if I'm trying to put unstable middle-of-the-night disasters on the robot.
turns.utterance: That study really made me think we shouldn't wait for national guidance to start learning locally. I think we should at least brainstorm a small robotic pathway for emergency general surgery cases and see whether there's a sensible pilot we could stand up here.

turns.inner_thought: I'm open, but only if this doesn't sound like we're trying to force the robot into the true emergency add-on stream without a plan. If they're talking about emergency cases, leadership will immediately think nights, weekends, same-day access, staffing, room assignment, and throughput disruption. I need an operational story that works inside current add-on flow, not a concept that depends on exceptions nobody has approved.
turns.utterance: I'm open to it, especially if we can define where emergency cases might realistically fit into our current add-on flow. If we bring anything forward, it has to read as operationally credible, not just clinically interesting.

turns.inner_thought: Best to keep this tightly selected: colectomies for contained perforation or obstruction, and some hernias where the imaging and physiology are favorable. That's the kind of small pilot that can actually succeed and avoid a string of conversions or delays. I definitely do not want the whole acute care service judged on every consult up front.
turns.utterance: I agree. If we do anything, I would start with colectomies for the right obstruction or perforation scenarios and selected hernias. That feels like the safest way to start with a small pilot before we talk about anything broader across the emergency service.

turns.inner_thought: That works for me if the pilot frame is broad enough to monitor the service line, not just the cases that actually get the robot. For committee review, we need to know the overall emergency colectomy and hernia volume, how often robotic use was possible, and whether it changed throughput. Otherwise it will look cherry-picked.
turns.utterance: A small pilot makes sense. We could track colectomy and hernia emergency cases across the service line and then see, within that pilot, whether robotics changes throughput in a meaningful way.

turns.inner_thought: The strongest argument clinically is lower conversion to open and better postoperative recovery. If we can show fewer open cases and a shorter postoperative stay, especially after colectomy, that's exactly the kind of signal that would make colleagues take this seriously. Preop waiting time is a separate issue and mostly unrelated to approach.
turns.utterance: From my perspective, the most attractive signal is lower conversion to open and potentially a shorter length of stay, especially if patients are recovering faster after minimally invasive colectomy.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, but leadership is going to translate that into total hospitalization. If length of stay doesn't move at the whole-stay level, it's hard to claim bed impact or financial value. I need this framed in a way that connects to boarding, capacity, and throughput dashboards, not just surgical recovery metrics.
turns.utterance: Right, and that's the piece leadership will latch onto. If the pilot can show a shorter length of stay and that translates into beds turning over sooner and less downstream pressure, then the story gets a lot stronger.

turns.inner_thought: Operationally, this is workable if we use the robot selectively in the patients who can wait until daylight after overnight resuscitation and optimization. In my mind, that's still an emergency case, and those next-morning slots are exactly where underused or releasable elective robot time can often be coordinated informally. I don't need a new policy to test a few cases.
turns.utterance: I think the pilot becomes much more realistic if we keep it simple and use the robot when it's available, particularly for urgent cases where we have a little time to get people ready. That would let us test the concept without overengineering it.

turns.inner_thought: If we're saying we'll use the robot when it's available, I need to translate that into current-state logistics: add-on staffing, room turnover, and where unscheduled robotic work could fit after the elective schedule is set. I cannot assume block sharing or informal releases; if this reaches the committee, I need it to sound feasible without special exceptions.
turns.utterance: Yes, in principle that's the right framing. If we're going to say we'll use the robot when it's available, then I think we should map the add-on staffing pattern and turnover windows so the committee can see that the idea is feasible.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll keep the proposal centered on emergency colectomy and hernia cases and make clear that robotic use would be selective and done by the acute care surgeons who already know the platform. That protects the pilot from looking like a training exercise or a wholesale service expansion.
turns.utterance: Why don't I draft a concept note around emergency colectomy and hernia cases, with selective robotic use by the acute care surgeons who are already credentialed on the platform? That should keep it focused and easier to review.

turns.inner_thought: That's enough for a first pass. I want a one-pager that gives emergency case volume, the length-of-stay opportunity in terms leadership recognizes, and a careful description of robot availability that stays within existing operations. If that lands well, we can decide whether a more formal pilot design is worth building.
turns.utterance: That sounds like a good next step. Let's bring forward a one-page pilot concept that highlights emergency case volume, the length-of-stay opportunity, and how robot availability could be described to the committee. If that narrative hangs together, we'll have something useful for the executive discussion.
